Simulation-Based Power Analysis

Part 8: Power analysis across varying sample sizes and effect sizes — Handout

Author
Affiliation

26 May 2026

1 From a point estimate to a power curve

Up to Part 7 we have computed power at one specific combination of design parameters (n, effect size, number of items, random-effects variances). That is useful but limited.

The standard deliverable for a sample-size justification — in a research proposal, a pre-registration, or a grant — is a power curve: power estimates across a range of sample sizes, often for several plausible effect sizes.

In this part we build:

  • A first power grid: power as a function of N subjects, for three effect sizes.
  • A second power grid: power as a function of both N subjects and N items, for a fixed (small) effect size.

We also add 95% confidence intervals on every power estimate, using the Clopper-Pearson exact binomial method. Each power value is itself the mean of 1000 binary outcomes (significant / not significant), so it has its own sampling uncertainty.

2 Recap of the generative model and one-dataset workflow

The data-generating function from Part 7:

# 7 model parameters (all on log scale):
b0       <- 6.59  # grand mean log(RT); exp(6.59) ~ 730 ms
b1       <- 0.10  # log-scale frequency effect (~70 ms on RT scale)
sigma_u0 <- 0.2   # SD of subject random intercepts
sigma_u1 <- 0.02  # SD of subject random slopes
rho      <- -0.5  # correlation between subject intercepts and slopes
sigma_w  <- 0.1   # SD of item random intercepts
sigma    <- 0.25  # residual SD

We will walk through generating one dataset step by step to make sure the pieces are clear, then wrap everything in gendat_ldt_crossed_log() and start iterating.

gendat_ldt_crossed_log <- function(n        = 20,
                                   k        = 20,
                                   b0       = 6.59,
                                   b1       = 0.10,
                                   sigma_u0 = 0.2,
                                   sigma_u1 = 0.02,
                                   rho      = -0.5,
                                   sigma_w  = 0.1,
                                   sigma    = 0.25) {

  sim_dat          <- expand.grid(item = 1:(k * 2), subj = 1:n)
  sim_dat$cond.cod <- rep(c(-0.5, 0.5), each = k)

  Sigma_u <- matrix(c(sigma_u0^2,                  rho * sigma_u0 * sigma_u1,
                      rho * sigma_u0 * sigma_u1,   sigma_u1^2),
                    nrow = 2)
  u <- mvrnorm(n = length(unique(sim_dat$subj)), mu = c(0, 0), Sigma = Sigma_u)
  w <- rnorm(n  = length(unique(sim_dat$item)), mean = 0, sd = sigma_w)

  N  <- dim(sim_dat)[1]
  rt <- rep(NA, N)
  for (i in 1:N) {
    rt[i] <- rlnorm(1,
                    b0 +
                    u[sim_dat[i, ]$subj, 1] +
                    w[sim_dat[i, ]$item] +
                    (b1 + u[sim_dat[i, ]$subj, 2]) * sim_dat[i, ]$cond.cod,
                    sigma)
  }

  sim_dat$rt   <- rt
  sim_dat$subj <- factor(sim_dat$subj)
  sim_dat$item <- factor(sim_dat$item)
  sim_dat
}

2.1 Sanity check on the generator

sim_dat <- gendat_ldt_crossed_log(n = 100, k = 100)
hist(sim_dat$rt, breaks = 50,
     main = "Distribution of Simulated RTs",
     xlab = "RT (ms)")

2.3 Sanity check on the model

Fit the model once and verify the fixed-effect estimates are near the true generating values:

m <- lmer(log(rt) ~ cond.cod + (1 + cond.cod | subj) + (1 | item), sim_dat,
          control = lmerControl(calc.derivs = FALSE))

3 Two power grids

We build two complementary power grids, presented in parallel tabs below.

The first grid varies subjects × effect sizes (with items fixed) — this is the standard “how many subjects do I need at each plausible effect size?” question. The second grid varies subjects × items (with effect size fixed at the small value) — useful when stimulus pool size is a design lever you control, common in psycholinguistics.

Both grids share the same machinery: build a parameter grid, run a nested power-simulation loop, load the precomputed result, compute Clopper-Pearson confidence intervals on each power estimate, and visualise. Each tab is self-contained.

Note

Confidence intervals on power. Each power estimate is the proportion of nsim independent significant results — a binomial proportion. The Clopper-Pearson method gives an exact confidence interval for that proportion. We define the helper calculate_power_ci() once here and reuse it in both tabs.

Show code (CI helper function) 
calculate_power_ci <- function(n_significant, n_total, conf.level = 0.95) {
  if (is.na(n_significant) || is.na(n_total) || n_total == 0) {
    return(c(power = NA, lower = NA, upper = NA))
  }
  n_significant <- as.integer(round(n_significant))
  n_total       <- as.integer(round(n_total))
  if (n_significant < 0)        n_significant <- 0
  if (n_significant > n_total)  n_significant <- n_total

  test_result <- binom.test(n_significant, n_total, conf.level = conf.level)
  c(power = unname(test_result$estimate),
    lower = test_result$conf.int[1],
    upper = test_result$conf.int[2])
}
  • First grid: subjects × effect sizes
  • Second grid: subjects × items (small effect)

The first power curve varies the number of subjects across three effect sizes, with items fixed at 40 per condition:

n_subj       <- c(24, 36, 48, 60, 72, 84, 96)
effect_sizes <- c(0.06, 0.10, 0.14)
n_item       <- 40  # fixed number of items per condition

power_grid       <- expand.grid(n = n_subj, b1 = effect_sizes)
power_grid$power <- NA

Each row of power_grid is one (n, effect) combination. We will fill in the power column by running nsim = 1000 simulations per row.

nsim <- 1000
nrow(power_grid)         # number of (n, effect) combinations
[1] 21
nrow(power_grid) * nsim  # total number of model fits
[1] 21000
Warning

21,000 model fits is a lot of computation. The full first grid takes ~5.34 hours on a standard laptop. Below we show the loop code (set to eval: false) and instead load the precomputed result.

3.0.1 The simulation loop

tic()
for (row in 1:nrow(power_grid)) {
  n_subj <- power_grid$n[row]
  effect <- power_grid$b1[row]

  message(sprintf("Running: n=%d, b1=%.2f (%d/%d)",
                  n_subj, effect, row, nrow(power_grid)))

  pvals <- rep(NA, nsim)
  for (i in 1:nsim) {
    sim_dat <- gendat_ldt_crossed_log(n = n_subj, k = n_item,
                                      b0 = 6.59, b1 = effect,
                                      sigma_u0 = 0.2, sigma_u1 = 0.02,
                                      rho = -0.5, sigma_w = 0.1, sigma = 0.25)
    m <- lmer(log(rt) ~ cond.cod + (1 + cond.cod | subj) + (1 | item), sim_dat,
              control = lmerControl(calc.derivs = FALSE))
    pvals[i] <- summary(m)$coefficients[2, 5]
  }
  power_grid$power[row] <- mean(pvals < 0.05)
}
toc() # 19246.916 sec elapsed = 5.34h

3.0.3 Add confidence intervals

Show code (CI computation) 
power_grid$n_sig    <- round(power_grid$power * nsim)
power_grid$lower_ci <- NA
power_grid$upper_ci <- NA

for (row in 1:nrow(power_grid)) {
  ci <- calculate_power_ci(power_grid$n_sig[row], nsim)
  power_grid$lower_ci[row] <- ci["lower"]
  power_grid$upper_ci[row] <- ci["upper"]
}

3.0.4 Visualisation: power curves

Show code (ggplot recipe) 
power_grid$effect_label <- factor(power_grid$b1,
                                  levels = c(0.06, 0.10, 0.14),
                                  labels = c("Small (b1=0.06)",
                                             "Medium (b1=0.10)",
                                             "Large (b1=0.14)"))

ggplot(power_grid, aes(x = n, y = power,
                       color = effect_label, fill = effect_label,
                       group = effect_label)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower_ci, ymax = upper_ci),
              alpha = 0.2, color = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.80, linetype = "dashed", color = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.95, linetype = "dashed", color = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = n_subj) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values  = c("#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73")) +
  labs(title    = "Power Curves with 95% Confidence Intervals",
       subtitle = sprintf("%d simulations per point", nsim),
       x        = "Number of Subjects",
       y        = "Statistical Power (1 - β)",
       color    = "Effect Size",
       fill     = "Effect Size") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(legend.position  = "bottom",
        plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold"),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

How to read this plot:

  • x-axis: number of subjects.
  • y-axis: power. Dashed lines mark the 80% and 95% conventional targets.
  • Three curves: power as a function of subjects for the three effect sizes.
  • Shaded ribbons: 95% Clopper-Pearson CIs on each power estimate.

A larger effect needs fewer subjects. Smaller effects need many more. The curve shape (S-curve flattening out near 1) is typical.

What if we instead want to understand how the number of items per condition trades off against the number of subjects, for a fixed (small) effect?

sample_sizes_2d <- c(24, 36, 48, 60, 72, 84, 96)
item_numbers_2d <- c(40, 60, 80, 100, 120)
effect_fixed    <- 0.06

power_grid_2d       <- expand.grid(n = sample_sizes_2d, nitem = item_numbers_2d)
power_grid_2d$power <- NA

nsim <- 500 # fewer simulations per cell for this larger grid
nrow(power_grid_2d) * nsim  # total simulations
[1] 17500
Warning

This second grid covers \(7 \times 5 = 35\) cells with 500 simulations each — 17,500 model fits. It took ~8.37 hours to run, so once again we show the loop and load the precomputed result.

3.0.5 The simulation loop

tic()
for (row in 1:nrow(power_grid_2d)) {
  n_subj  <- power_grid_2d$n[row]
  n_items <- power_grid_2d$nitem[row]

  message(sprintf("Running: n=%d, k=%d (%d/%d)",
                  n_subj, n_items, row, nrow(power_grid_2d)))

  pvals <- rep(NA, nsim)
  for (i in 1:nsim) {
    sim_dat <- gendat_ldt_crossed_log(n = n_subj, k = n_items,
                                      b0 = 6.59, b1 = effect_fixed,
                                      sigma_u0 = 0.2, sigma_u1 = 0.02,
                                      rho = -0.5, sigma_w = 0.1, sigma = 0.25)
    m <- lmer(log(rt) ~ cond.cod + (1 + cond.cod | subj) + (1 | item), sim_dat,
              control = lmerControl(calc.derivs = FALSE))
    pvals[i] <- summary(m)$coefficients[2, 5]
  }
  power_grid_2d$power[row] <- mean(pvals < 0.05)
}

power_grid_2d$upper_ci <- NA

for (row in 1:nrow(power_grid_2d)) {
  if (!is.na(power_grid_2d$power[row])) {
    ci <- calculate_power_ci(power_grid_2d$n_sig[row], nsim)
    power_grid_2d$lower_ci[row] <- ci["lower"]

3.0.8 Visualisation: heatmap

Show code (ggplot recipe) 
ggplot(power_grid_2d, aes(x = factor(n), y = factor(nitem), fill = power)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", size = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", power)),
            color = "black", size = 5, fontface = "bold", vjust = -0.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", lower_ci, upper_ci)),
            color = "grey40", size = 3, vjust = 1.2) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low      = "#d73027",
                       mid      = "#fee08b",
                       high     = "#1a9850",
                       midpoint = 0.80,
                       limits   = c(0, 1),
                       breaks   = seq(0, 1, 0.2),
                       name     = "Power") +
  labs(title    = "Power as a Function of Subjects and Items",
       subtitle = sprintf("Effect size: b1 = %.2f (log scale), %d simulations per point",
                          effect_fixed, nsim),
       x = "Number of Subjects",
       y = "Number of Items") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(plot.title  = element_text(face = "bold"),
        panel.grid  = element_blank())

The heatmap shows that both axes matter. To detect a small effect with adequate power, you can either run many subjects with moderate items, or fewer subjects with many items. The corner of the grid (96 subjects × 120 items per condition) is the easiest case.

4 What to do next

The power analysis above is intentionally coarse — three effect sizes in the first grid, seven subject counts × five item counts in the second. For an actual study planning exercise:

  • Zoom in on the range of (subjects, items) where you cross the 80% or 95% threshold.
  • Run more simulations per cell (e.g., 2000+ instead of 500) to tighten the CIs.
  • Refine the input parameters (\(\sigma_{u0}, \sigma_{u1}, \rho, \sigma_w, \sigma\)) from a pilot dataset rather than relying on values from the literature — they are the single biggest source of uncertainty in the result.

5 The final model

After eight parts we have built up a full data-generating process and a matching LMM:

\[ \log(rt_{ij}) = \beta_0 + u_{0i} + w_{0j} + (\beta_1 + u_{1i}) \times \text{cond.cod}_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij} \]

where \(\varepsilon_{ij} \sim \text{Normal}(0, \sigma)\),

\[ \begin{pmatrix} u_0 \\ u_1 \end{pmatrix} \sim \text{MVN} \left( \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \, \Sigma_u \right), \quad \Sigma_u = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_{u0}^2 & \rho \, \sigma_{u0} \sigma_{u1} \\ \rho \, \sigma_{u0} \sigma_{u1} & \sigma_{u1}^2 \end{pmatrix}, \]

and \(w_0 \sim \text{Normal}(0, \sigma_w)\).

Corresponding lmer() formula:

lmer(log(rt) ~ cond.cod + (1 + cond.cod | subj) + (1 | item), data = ...)

6 Where to go next

This course covered simulation-based power analysis in R using lme4. Two recommended next steps:

  • Vasishth & Nicenboim, Using simulation to understand your model — Freq_CogSci. Same paradigm, more examples, written for psycholinguistics.
  • Julia + MixedModelsSim.jl — simulation tutorial. Julia is roughly 10-100× faster than R for these simulations, which makes it feasible to scan much larger grids.
